hook_text: A broom, a traffic cone and a stack of books explain why a thirty metre tower stays up in a gale.
clip_script: Balance a ruler on your finger. That point is its centre of gravity, where all its weight acts. Now the rule: a thing stands as long as a line straight down from that point lands inside its base. Tilt a traffic cone and it rocks back; its centre of gravity is low and its base is wide. Stand a broom on the end of its handle and it topples; high centre of gravity, tiny base. Lean a stack of books and it falls the moment the balance point passes the bottom book's edge. A tower is tall, so its centre of gravity is high, and wind tilts it. The answers: a wide base, most of the steel low down, a heavy concrete foot that bolts it to the earth, and guy wires on thin masts. Then strengthen the weak spots: gusset plates across the corners, webs between bars, an X of bracing inside so it cannot twist. And one more problem no triangle solves: the neighbours do not want to look at it. So disguise it as a pine tree.
visual_style: Whiteboard cone, broom and book stack tilting with a dashed line from each centre of gravity; a tower with wide base, gussets and internal X, ending as a pine tree.
mood: Clear and a little playful, physics made visible with kitchen objects.
pacing: Three quick tilts, the one-line rule, the tower's answers, then the surprise of the disguised tree.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and find the centre of gravity of three objects on your desk.
